Potre Dirampatan-Diampuan
Dr. Potre Dirampatan-Diampuan (also indexed as Potre D.
Diampuan) is a Maranao educator, scholar, peacebuilder,
interfaith leader, and halal-policy practitioner from Mindanao,
Philippines.
For decades she's worked where Islamic scholarship,
education, governance, and community peace meet, and her
record now includes a doctoral dissertation, university-
published book chapters, a published policy essay, invited
lectures, and a growing body of research that cites her work.
She serves as CEO of the Alliance for Halal Integrity in the
Philippines Inc. (AHIP), served as a Global Council Trustee
of the United Religions Initiative (URI) for Southeast Asia
and the Pacific from 2018 to 2022, and co-authored a 2021
chapter that proposed five principles of moral governance for
the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM).

BACKGROUND
Dr. Potre is rooted in Marawi City and the wider Lanao area,
and her Maranao heritage sits at the center of her work.
That background isn't cultural decoration. It's the base for her
thinking on Muslim identity, autonomy, and coexistence in a
diverse and often tense archipelago.
After the 2017 Marawi siege, she spoke about the longing of
displaced residents to rebuild their homes and lives with
dignity.
Her own family's story includes displacement during past
conflicts, and that lived experience has kept her wary of top-
down "solutions" and committed to slower, trust-based work
across faith lines.
EDUCATION
She earned her Ph.D. in Educational Management from
Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City.
Her doctoral dissertation, Understanding Jihad: Basis for
Policy Formulation and Educational Programs for Muslims
in the Philippines (2006), is cataloged by the Philippine eLib
under the subjects Jihad, Education and state, and Muslims,
Education, Philippines.[1]
The study's analysis of greater (inner) and lesser (physical) jihad was later used in educational material on Islam
and peace.[2]
She also holds a master's degree in School Administration from MSU and another in Cultural Anthropology from
the University of the Philippines.
In 2005, she was a British Council Fellow at the University of Durham in the United Kingdom, an experience that
broadened her view of peacebuilding and dialogue.
Her author biography in Development for Peace lists her writing interests as Muslim institutions in Philippine
bureaucracy, sustainable peace, development, and governance.[3]
CAREER
Education and Peacebuilding in the Classroom
Dr. Potre treats education as a frontline tool for peace.
She's trained teachers to bring peacebuilding into everyday instruction, consulted on Muslim education initiatives
for the Department of Education, and advised local government in Marawi.

A 2024 research article on women leaders in Mindanao highlights her peacebuilding work in curricula and teacher
training.[4]
Scarboro Missions documented her use of the Golden Rule poster in peace-education and interfaith programs,
including engagement with the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs.[5]
Interfaith Leadership and the United Religions Initiative
The United Religions Initiative (URI) appointed her Regional Coordinator for Southeast Asia and the Pacific
around 2012.
She later served as Senior Interfaith Advisor for the Philippines and as Global Council Trustee for Southeast Asia
and the Pacific from 2018 to 2022.[6]
URI's 2013 to 2014 organizational review records her perspective on conflict, peace, and the Bangsamoro peace
process as regional coordinator, and a 2018 "Every Voice" profile describes her interfaith philosophy.[7][8]
In 2012, she organized a United Nations International Day of Peace observance at a Taguig City mosque under the
theme "Sustainable Peace for a Sustainable Future," which drew about 500 people.[9]
Her name also appears among Philippine participants in United Nations documentation for the 2011 Commission
on the Status of Women (E/CN.6/2011/INF/1), though the record misprints her honorific.[10]
UK-Philippines Partners for Peace and the NCMF
She co-founded the United Kingdom-Philippines Partners for Peace (UKPPP) with other Mindanao scholars,
backed by the British Council, to support peace efforts back home.
For the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), she has consulted on peace programs and on
preventing and countering violent extremism (PCVE).
Halal Industry Advocacy and AHIP
As CEO of AHIP, Dr. Potre pushes for stronger halal standards, education, certification, and regulatory
frameworks.
Her point is simple: halal integrity has to hold at every stage, from raw materials to the finished product, and
getting it right helps Muslim communities while opening doors for Philippine goods abroad.
In 2024, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) named her among the leaders of halal-certifying bodies who
took part in a government-industry dialogue.[11]
A 2019 study on halal certification among non-halal restaurant owners in Manila also cites her as an AHIP
authority on the regulatory setting.[12]

SCHOLARLY WORKS
Doctoral Dissertation (2006)
Understanding Jihad is her foundational academic work. It argues for policy and educational programs for
Muslims in the Philippines grounded in a careful reading of jihad, and the 2021 moral governance chapter cites it.
[1][3]
Iran's Islamic Revolution and Filipino People Power (2017)
In "A Theoretical Study: Iran's Islamic Revolution and the Filipino People Power," she compares six theoretical
explanations of the Iranian Revolution with the Philippine People Power Revolution and maps where the two
converge and diverge.
The chapter appears on pages 50 to 62 of Philippine-Iran Relations: 50 Years and Beyond, edited by H. A. Sevilla
Jr. and published by the Asian Center, University of the Philippines Diliman.[13]
Moral Governance in the Bangsamoro (2021)
Co-authored with Dr. Nassef Manabilang Adiong, "Principles and Practice of Moral Governance in the
Bangsamoro" appears on pages 31 to 53 of Development for Peace, edited by U. S. Malik and published by MSU-
Marawi and Maven Media Asia.[3]
It's an exploratory, conceptual piece that asks how BARMM can move past secular "good governance" toward a
faith-informed moral governance built on five linked principles: Faith, Freedom, Moral Authority, Common Good,
and Social Ethics.
The framework draws on Islamic values while staying inclusive of Christians, Indigenous Peoples, and every other
group in the region.
It also takes on BARMM's practical problems: corruption legacies from the old ARMM era, the need for merit-
based systems, and accountable leadership.
Halal Policy Essay (2023)
On November 24, 2023, BusinessWorld published her essay "Gaps in the Halal Industry in the Philippines: Call for
Legislating Philippine Halal Authority."
She argues for a dedicated national halal agency with both regulatory and development functions. It's a policy
essay, not a peer-reviewed journal article, and it was also republished by HalalFocus.[14]
RECEPTION AND CITATIONS
Her work has traveled well beyond its original pages, and the moral governance chapter in particular has become a
reference point in Bangsamoro governance discussions.

A 2025 study on moral governance and school heads' performance in the Bangsamoro Special Geographic

Her 2017 Iran chapter is also cited in a peer-reviewed article by H. A. Sevilla Jr. on Philippine-Iran relations in

[21]
Her dissertation also appears in the bibliography of the Sampung Piling Salitang Meranao and in the references of

SCHOLARSHIP ABOUT HER
The 2024 article "Emanating Change: Fragments of Micro-Empowerment Among Women Leaders in Mindanao,
Philippines" studies twelve women leaders in the region, and Dr. Potre is one of them.
It treats her as a Meranaw educator and peacebuilder and discusses her peacebuilding in curricula and teacher
training, her grassroots work, the UK-Philippines Partners for Peace, her British Council fellowship, and her
interfaith leadership.[4]
LECTURES AND INTERFAITH CONTRIBUTIONS
"Revisiting the Narrative of Bangsamoro" (January 27, 2022): an invited virtual lecture for the Policy
Research and Legal Services of the Bangsamoro Parliament, covering Bangsamoro ethnolinguistic groups
and identity, narratives and historicity of Muslims in the Philippines, and a chronicle of Muslim affairs.[22]
Muslim contribution to the Interfaith Forum on Laudato Si (2016, Malate Parish, Manila): her
intervention connected religion, human development, climate change, sustainability, and the
interconnectedness of people and the planet.[23]
"Interfaith and the Future of Our Earth" (2013, Pasay City): she hosted this URI Southeast Asia and the
Pacific roundtable on how different faiths approach protecting the planet.[24]
"How I Came Into Interfaith" (2014): she interviewed Dr. Noemi Medina for the URI Southeast Asia-
Pacific archive, a documented oral-history contribution rather than a scholarly publication.[25]
LEGACY
Dr. Potre's career is a study in persistence and range.

title: Datu Abul Khayr Dangcal Alonto
text:
PAGE 1
DATU ABUL KHAYR DANGCAL
ALONTO:

FROM MNLF COMMANDER TO ARCHITECT OF MINDANAO
DEVELOPMENT

Ashary Tamano
CESO IV, I.T. Specialist, Planner, Researcher


PAGE 2
INTRODUCTION

The modern political history of Mindanao cannot be told without confronting a difficult
transformation: how a generation of Moro revolutionaries moved from armed struggle to
institutional governance. Some resisted that transition. Some were overtaken by it. A few
managed to navigate both worlds—carrying the legitimacy of rebellion into the machinery of the

state.
Datu Abul Khayr Dangceal Alonto (1945-2019) belonged to that smaller, more complex category.

He was not merely a participant in the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF); he was part of
its early command structure, one of the original “Top 90” trainees who formed the backbone of
the movement’s armed wing. He rose to become Vice Chairman of the organization during a
formative and volatile period. Yet his life did not remain confined to insurgency. Over the
decades, he would become an elected local executive in Marawi City, a figure in autonomy
institutions, a diplomat representing the Republic of the Philippines abroad, a factional leader
navigating internal Moro political fractures, and eventually Chairperson of the Mindanao

Development Authority (MinDA) at Cabinet rank.

Few careers in Bangsamoro history illustrate so vividly the passage from rebellion to

governance.

Alonto’s trajectory is not a simple story of conversion—from fighter to peacemaker. It is more
layered than that. It reflects the internal evolution of the Moro struggle itself: the realization that
armed confrontation, while historically catalytic, could not by itself secure lasting political and
economic transformation. Institutions, budgets, infrastructure, and development planning would

eventually become as decisive as battlefield strategy.

This article reconstructs that arc. Drawing from contemporary reporting, institutional records,
peace-process analyses, and Bangsamoro transitional documents, it traces Alonto’s life across
five distinct but interconnected phases: early formation in Marawi; revolutionary mobilization
and armed leadership; political realignment and autonomy engagement; diplomatic and national
roles; and finally, development-centered governance through MinDA. It situates his choices
within broader historical contexts—martial law, the Tripoli Agreement, MNLF fragmentation,

and the long road to the Bangsamoro political settlement.


PAGE 3
To understand Alonto is to understand a generation forced to negotiate between memory and

pragmatism, between dignity and compromise, between war and institution-building.

I. FAMILY BACKGROUND AND EARLY LIFE IN
MARAWI

Abul Khayr Dangeal Alonto was born in 1945 in Marawi City, at a moment of national
transition. The Second World War had just ended. The Philippines was rebuilding. In Mindanao,
however, older tensions were quietly intensifying. Demographic shifts, land resettlement
policies, and state integration projects were reshaping the balance between indigenous Muslim

communities and incoming settlers.

Marawi was not merely a geographic birthplace. It was the intellectual and political center of the
Maranao people. Historically known as Dansalan before its renaming, it had long served as a
bastion of Islamic scholarship, aristocratic lineage networks, and resistance to colonial
penetration. Spanish forces had struggled to subdue it. American administrators eventually
established presence, but never fully dissolved its internal power structures. Even into the mid-
twentieth century, Marawi retained a strong sense of distinct identity within the Philippine
republic.

Alonto was born into one of its prominent families.

His father, Abdul Ghaffur Madki Alangadi Alonto, had served as provincial governor and later as
a Philippine ambassador. His mother, Bai Hajja Rasmia Indol Dangeal, came from another
respected Maranao lineage. Politics, therefore, was not a distant subject discussed in newspapers;
it was embedded in daily life. Governance, negotiation, and representation were familiar

conversations within the household.

This upbringing gave Alonto two forms of capital. First, social capital: access to networks across
clan structures and political institutions. Second, political literacy: an early understanding of how

power operates within both local and national arenas.

Yet growing up in a politically connected family during the 1950s and 1960s also meant

witnessing contradictions. While certain Maranao elites maintained influence, broader Moro


PAGE 4
communities were increasingly experiencing marginalization. State-sponsored migration from
Luzon and the Visayas altered land ownership patterns in Mindanao. Tensions over ancestral
domains intensified. Armed settler groups emerged in some areas. Economic development

programs often bypassed Muslim-majority provinces.
‘These developments formed the backdrop of Alonto’s formative years.

He pursued higher education beyond Mindanao, studying political science at Cairo University.
Cairo during the 1960s was a center of post-colonial discourse. Arab nationalism, Islamic
political thought, and Third World solidarity movements were intellectually vibrant. For a young
Moro student, exposure to these currents offered language and theoretical framing for grievances
already felt at home. Concepts such as self-determination, anti-imperialism, and national

liberation were not abstract—they resonated directly with the Bangsamoro condition.

Upon returning to the Philippines, Alonto also undertook legal studies at San Beda College. This
legal training would later prove significant. It sharpened his appreciation for institutional
frameworks and constitutional mechanisms—knowledge that would become increasingly
relevant as the Moro struggle moved from purely armed confrontation toward negotiations and

autonomy design.
However, it was not academic exposure alone that propelled him toward activism.

The late 1960s witnessed the eruption of the Jabidah controversy, involving the reported killing
of Muslim military trainees. Whether examined through investigative journalism or oral
accounts, the incident had a profound psychological impact on Muslim communities. For many
young Moro intellectuals, it symbolized systemic disregard for Muslim lives and deepened

distrust of central authorities.
Alonto belonged to this generation.

In response to the growing sense of injustice, he became involved in organizing Muslim youth.
One of the formations associated with this period was LAM ALIF, a youth organization
composed of politically conscious Muslim students and activists. Several of its members would

later emerge as key figures within the Moro National Liberation Front.


PAGE 5
The trajectory from youth organizing to armed movement was not instantaneous, but it was
increasingly foreseeable. By the end of the 1960s, peaceful appeals were widely perceived as
insufficient. Structural grievances—land dispossession, political underrepresentation, communal

violence—were intensifying rather than easing.

For Alonto and his contemporaries, the question was no longer whether change was needed, but

how it would be pursued.

The answer, in time, would take him far from the lecture halls of Cairo and Manila—into the

ranks of a revolutionary organization that would reshape Mindanao’s political history.

IL POLITICAL AWAKENING AND ENTRY INTO THE
MORO NATIONAL LIBERATION FRONT

By the close of the 1960s, political consciousness among Moro youth had moved beyond
scattered protest and campus-based discussion. What had begun as localized expressions of
grievance was slowly coalescing into a broader nationalist imagination. For young activists like
Abul Khayr Dangeal Alonto, the question was no longer whether the Bangsamoro people were

oppressed; the question was what form organized resistance should take.
Several forces converged to shape this moment.

First, the memory of Jabidah continued to circulate, reinforced by new stories of military abuses,
land grabbing, and communal violence. These narratives were not isolated rumors but lived
realities for families in Cotabato, Lanao, Sulu, and Zamboanga. Second, a growing number of
Moro students were returning from abroad—particularly from the Middle East—bringing with
them exposure to anti-colonial movements and liberation struggles in Asia and Africa. Third,
informal networks of Muslim intellectuals, ulama, and community leaders were quietly debating

the possibility of a unified Moro political organization.
Alonto stood at the intersection of these currents.

His earlier involvement in Muslim youth organizing placed him in contact with individuals who

were already moving toward clandestine coordination. These were not yet soldiers; they were


PAGE 6
organizers, couriers, and political educators. Meetings were small, discreet, and often framed as
study sessions or community consultations. But beneath the surface, a strategic shift was

underway.

The idea gaining traction was radical for its time: that Moros constituted a nation, and that this

nation had the right to self-determination.

‘This framing departed from earlier Muslim political approaches that sought accommodation
within the Philippine state through elite bargaining. Instead, it articulated a collective identity

rooted in shared history, religion, territory, and experience of marginalization.

When the Moro National Liberation Front formally emerged as an organized movement in the
early 1970s, Alonto was already part of its inner circle. His combination of education, political

maturity, and family connections made him a natural recruit for leadership responsibilities.

Unlike mass-based recruitment later in the conflict, early MNLF recruitment was highly
selective. Prospective members were screened not only for commitment, but for discipline and

discretion. The movement understood that premature exposure could lead to swift suppression.

Alonto’s entry into the MNLF was therefore not a spontaneous act. It was the culmination of

years of political evolution.
He was not joining an existing army.
He was helping to build one.

At this stage, the MNLF was still more political organization than military force. Its early
emphasis lay in ideological consolidation, organizational design, and external linkages—

particularly with Muslim countries sympathetic to anti-colonial struggles.

Alonto’s role during this period leaned toward political-military integration. He participated in
discussions about strategy, organizational hierarchy, and recruitment patterns. Even before

formal combat operations began, he was being prepared for command responsibility.

This preparation would soon become explicit.


PAGE 7
II. THE “TOP 90” AND THE FORMATION OF A
REVOLUTIONARY CADRE

In 1969, a pivotal decision was made by emerging MNLF leadership: a select group of recruits
would be sent abroad for intensive guerrilla warfare training. This group would later be

remembered as the “Top 90.”
Abul Khayr Dangcal Alonto was among them.

The existence of the Top 90 reflects a crucial strategic insight. The MNLF did not intend to rely
solely on spontaneous uprising. It sought to create a disciplined core of cadres who could serve

as trainers, organizers, and commanders once armed struggle expanded.

Training reportedly took place in Pulau Pangkor, Malaysia, and lasted roughly a year. Details
about the curriculum remain limited in public sources, partly because secrecy was an essential
component of survival. What can be reasonably inferred from later accounts is that the training

combined:

+ Basic guerrilla tactics
+ Weapons handling

+ Small-unit organization
+ Political education

+ Revolutionary discipline
The emphasis was not merely on fighting, but on building a movement.
For Alonto, this experience represented a decisive turning point.

He was no longer only an activist or student of politics. He was being transformed into a

revolutionary officer.

Equally important was the composition of the Top 90 itself. The cohort included Moros from
different ethnolinguistic groups—Maranao, Maguindanao, Tausug, Sama, and others. This
diversity reflected the MNLF’s aspiration to transcend local identities and forge a unified

Bangsamoro struggle.


PAGE 8
Living, training, and struggling together in a foreign environment fostered a sense of shared
destiny among the trainees. These bonds would later shape leadership relationships, alliances,

and rivalries within the movement.

Upon completion of training, Alonto and his fellow Top 90 members returned to Mindanao not

as anonymous recruits, but as foundational pillars of the emerging armed wing.
Alonto was assigned to the Lanao area, where he would assume field command responsibilities.
His ascent within the organization was rapid.

He became recognized not only as a capable commander, but as a political figure within the
movement. Eventually, he would be elevated to Vice Chairman of the MNLF, placing him
directly beneath Nur Misuari in the early leadership hierarchy.

This dual status—military commander and senior political officer—was significant. It meant that

Alonto participated in both battlefield planning and strategic policy discussions.

The war, from his vantage point, was inseparable from politics.

IV. ROLE IN THE EARLY ARMED STRUGGLE

When open hostilities erupted in the early 1970s, the MNLF faced an enormous challenge. It
confronted a centralized state with superior firepower, air assets, and formal military
infrastructure. What the movement possessed instead was popular support in certain areas,

familiarity with terrain, and the commitment of its cadres.

As commander of MNLF forces in Lanao, Alonto operated in one of the conflict’s most sensitive

theaters.

Lanao was densely populated, politically complex, and deeply embedded in clan networks.
Military action in such an environment could not be separated from social consequences. A.

single clash could ripple outward into clan feuds, displacement, and cycles of retaliation.

Alonto’s responsibilities therefore extended beyond tactical engagements. He had to manage

relationships with community elders, religious leaders, and local commanders. He had to ensure


PAGE 9
discipline among fighters. He had to navigate the fine line between revolutionary necessity and

civilian protection.

Contemporary peace-process analyses describe him as one of the principal early field
commanders tasked with territorial responsibilities. This placed him among a small group of

leaders who bore the burden of translating national-level directives into local operational reality.

Accounts from later years suggest that Alonto’s leadership style during this period emphasized
organization and coordination rather than indiscriminate violence. While war inevitably involved
bloodshed, the strategic goal remained political: to pressure the Philippine state into recognizing

the Bangsamoro cause.

By the mid-1970s, however, it had become clear that armed struggle alone would not produce
decisive victory. The state was not collapsing. International support was uneven. Civilians were

bearing heavy costs.

It was in this context that new pathways began to emerge.


PAGE 10
V. VICE MAYORSHIP, ACTING MAYORSHIP, AND
TURN TO THE UNDERGROUND

One of the most revealing episodes in Abul Khayr Dangcal Alonto’s political life is the period
when he simultaneously inhabited two worlds: formal local governance and underground

revolutionary struggle.

In 1972, Alonto ran for Vice Mayor of Marawi City and won by an overwhelming margin. He
was widely regarded as one of the youngest city executives in the country at that time. The
victory was not accidental. It reflected both his family’s political standing and his growing

personal reputation as a principled, articulate, and capable leader.

At first glance, participation in electoral politics might appear inconsistent with membership in
an armed revolutionary organization. But within the political logic of the period, the two were

not mutually exclusive.

Many Moro leaders of Alonto’s generation viewed electoral office as another arena of struggle.

Holding local government positions allowed them to:

+ Protect communities from abuses where possible
+ Channel resources toward neglected areas
+ Build political legitimacy among constituents

+ Test whether meaningful reform within the system was still feasible

For Alonto, the vice mayoralty was not an abandonment of the MNLF cause. It was a tactical

extension of it.

In 1974, he briefly served as Acting Mayor of Marawi City. His assumption of this role placed
him in direct confrontation with the realities of governance under Martial Law. The Marcos
regime had centralized power, curtailed civil liberties, and empowered security forces with
sweeping authority. Reports of arbitrary arrests, disappearances, and torture were widespread,

particularly in Muslim areas.

The space for reformist local governance quickly shrank.


PAGE 11
Before he could be formally sworn in as full mayor, Alonto made a decisive choice. He left his

position and went underground to rejoin his MNLF comrades.

This move signaled a conclusion reached through experience: electoral participation under
Martial Law could not deliver the structural change that Moros sought. The political arena had

become too tightly controlled by the central regime.

Alonto’s return to clandestine activity also underscored a personal principle that would
characterize his career—he was willing to relinquish formal power when he believed it had

become morally or strategically meaningless.

The episode also cemented his reputation among MNLF ranks as a leader who did not use public
office as a shield from risk. He had already held power and given it up.

That mattered.

VI. INTERNAL MNLF FRACTURES AND STRATEGIC
REALIGNMENTS

By the late 1970s, the Moro National Liberation Front was no longer the unified organization it

had been during its early years.
Several fault lines had emerged:

+ Disagreements over leadership style
+ Divergent views on negotiations with the Marcos government
+ Tensions between centralized authority and regional commanders

+ Personal rivalries shaped by war-time experiences
‘These internal strains were intensified by external developments.

In 1976, the Tripoli Agreement was signed between the Philippine government and the MNLF,
brokered by the Organization of Islamic Conference. The agreement recognized the principle of

autonomy for Muslim Mindanao, marking the first major political concession to Moro demands.

However, implementation proved deeply contentious.


PAGE 12
Many within the MNLF viewed the Marcos government's version of autonomy as diluted and

insincere. Others believed that imperfect autonomy was preferable to endless war.
Within this context, Abul Khayr Alonto found himself navigating a complicated terrain.

In 1978, he was removed from the MNLF central committee by Nur Misuari. Shortly thereafter,

Alonto entered into a separate accommodation with the Marcos government.
This episode has often been simplified as defection or betrayal.
Amore careful reading suggests something more complex.

Alonto did not abandon the goal of Moro self-governance. Instead, he shifted his arena of

struggle from insurgency toward the emerging autonomy framework.

He became involved in the institutions created in the wake of the Tripoli Agreement. He served
as an assemblyman in the regional autonomous structure, later became interim head of a regional

autonomous government, and eventually served as Speaker of a regional legislative assembly.

These were fragile, contested institutions. They lacked stable resources and clear constitutional

footing. They were often overshadowed by continuing armed conflict.
Yet for leaders like Alonto, they represented a new battlefield.

Instead of commanding fighters, he now had to command budgets, legislative procedures, and

bureaucratic processes.
This transition required a different kind of discipline.
Former revolutionaries entering governance confronted immediate challenges:

+ Limited administrative experience
+ Patronage-driven polities
+ Weak institutional culture

+ Persistent suspicion from both government and rebel ranks

Alonto’s willingness to remain inside these imperfect structures suggests a strategic calculation.
He appeared to believe that autonomy, however flawed, provided a platform from which future

gains could be pursued.


PAGE 13
In this sense, his realignment did not mark an abandonment of the Moro struggle, but an.

evolution in its form.

From this point onward, Alonto increasingly defined his role as an institution-builder rather than

an insurgent commander.

VII. FROM REVOLUTIONARY TO AUTONOMY
INSTITUTION-BUILDER

By the early 1980s, Abul Khayr Dangcal Alonto had crossed a threshold that many former
revolutionaries struggle to navigate: he committed himself to the slow, frustrating, and often

thankless work of institution-building.
This shift did not occur overnight.

It emerged from cumulative experience—years of war, internal movement fractures, failed
ceasefires, and partial political settlements. Alonto had seen firsthand both the power and the
limits of armed struggle. He had also experienced the limits of symbolic political agreements that

were not matched by serious implementation.
Autonomy, imperfect as it was, offered a new terrain.

For Alonto, autonomy institutions were not end-goals. They were scaffolding—structures upon

which more meaningful self-governance might eventually be constructed.

As an assemblyman in the regional autonomous government and later as interim head and
Speaker of a regional legislative body, Alonto immersed himself in legislative work, policy
formulation, and administrative management. These roles demanded a very different skill set

from guerrilla command.
Instead of issuing battlefield orders, he now had to:

+ Negotiate with political rivals
+ Build coalitions inside legislative chambers
+ Interpret legal frameworks

+ Work within budget constraints


PAGE 14
+ Engage national agencies

This transition was not glamorous.
Early autonomy institutions were plagued by:
+ Weak funding
+ Ambiguous legal authority
+ Overlapping jurisdictions
+ Persistent interference from the central government

Many former revolutionaries grew disillusioned and returned to armed struggle or withdrew from
politics altogether.

Alonto did not.
He stayed.

His persistence suggests a long-term strategic orientation. He appeared to recognize that
sustainable political gains would only emerge through cumulative institutional practice, however
slow and imperfect.

This period also sharpened his understanding of governance realities. He witnessed how
patronage networks distorted policymaking. He observed how bureaucratic inertia could derail
even well-intentioned programs. He saw how the absence of professional civil service systems
undermined continuity.

‘These experiences would later inform his emphasis on development planning, inter-agency
coordination, and infrastructure-driven integration when he headed MinDA.

Ina sense, the autonomy years were Alonto’s apprenticeship in civilian statecraft.

VIII. DIPLOMATIC CAREER AND INTERNATIONAL ENGAGEMENT

In 1994, Abul Khayr Alonto was appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the
Republic of the Philippines to Nigeria and several other African states.

For a former MNLF commander, this appointment carried deep symbolic weight.

It represented the Philippine state’s formal recognition that former adversaries could be
legitimate representatives of national interests. It also reflected confidence in Alonto’s capacity
to operate within the norms of international diplomacy.

His diplomatic posting expanded his worldview further.


PAGE 15
Diplomacy exposed him to:
+ Multilateral negotiations
+ Development cooperation frameworks
+ Investment promotion strategies
+ Regional integration initiatives

These experiences reinforced a lesson he had already begun to internalize: political solutions
require economic foundations.

During this period, Alonto increasingly articulated Moro concerns not only in terms of historical
injustice, but also in terms of development deficits—poverty, infrastructure gaps, unemployment,
and lack of market access.

This framing did not replace identity-based claims. Instead, it complemented them.

The Bangsamoro struggle, in Alonto’s evolving view, was as much about building viable
economies as it was about asserting political rights.

His diplomatic service thus functioned as another stage in his transformation—from
revolutionary commander, to autonomy politician, to development-oriented statesman.

IX. RE-EMERGENCE IN MNLF LEADERSHIP AND PEACE ADVOCACY

Although Alonto had long been operating within government institutions, he never severed ties
with the broader Moro revolutionary community.

In 2014, amid leadership disputes within the MNLF following Nur Misuari’s political and
military setbacks, Alonto emerged as one of the figures asserting a claim to MNLF chairmanship.

More important than the title itself was his public position.

Alonto openly supported the peace process between the Philippine government and the Moro
Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), including the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law. He framed
peace not as surrender, but as strategic transition.

He argued that:
+ Armed struggle had fulfilled its historical role
+ The political battlefield had shifted

+ The future of the Bangsamoro lay in negotiated political settlements and democratic
ratification

Crucially, he emphasized peaceful, non-violent, Islamic, and democratic means of resolving
political disputes.


PAGE 16
This stance placed him firmly within the camp of revolutionary elders who accepted that the next
phase of struggle would be fought through legislation, plebiscites, and institution-building rather
than through armed confrontation.

It also reflected continuity rather than rupture.

From his early years, Alonto had always treated war as instrumental rather than romantic. His
later peace advocacy can therefore be understood as consistent with his long-held view that
political objectives, not perpetual conflict, were paramount.

X. CHAIRMANSHIP OF THE MINDANAO DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY AND
DEVELOPMENT VISION

In 2016, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Abul Khayr Dangcal Alonto as Chairperson of the
Mindanao Development Authority (MinDA), a Cabinet-rank position.

For Alonto, MinDA represented the culmination of decades of political evolution.
MinDA’s mandate is to accelerate Mindanao’s socioeconomic development by:

+ Promoting investments

+ Strengthening infrastructure

+ Enhancing inter-regional connectivity

+ Supporting peace and development initiatives
Alonto embraced a core proposition:

Peace will not survive without development.
Development will not succeed without peace.

Under his leadership, MinDA promoted the concept of Mindanao Development Corridors—
geographic growth zones designed to disperse economic activity beyond traditional urban
centers. The objective was to ensure that development benefits reached historically marginalized
areas, including conflict-affected provinces.

He also pushed for:
+ Expansion of ecozones
+ Strengthening of inter-island shipping routes
+ Advocacy for a Mindanao railway system

+ Active participation in the Brunei—Indonesia—Malaysia—Philippines East ASEAN Growth
Area (BIMP-EAGA)


PAGE 17
These initiatives were not abstract planning exercises. They were conceived as mechanisms to
physically and economically integrate Mindanao, reducing the isolation that had long fueled
underdevelopment and grievance.

Alonto frequently framed infrastructure as a unifying force. Roads, ports, and railways were not
merely economic assets; they were instruments of social cohesion.

In this sense, MinDA became Alonto’s final battlefield.
Not one of gunfire.

But one of blueprints, budgets, and inter-agency negotiations.

XI. LEADERSHIP STYLE AND IDEAS

Those who worked with Alonto often described him as soft-spoken, patient, and strategic.
He preferred persuasion to confrontation.

He was comfortable operating behind the scenes.

These traits were shaped by a lifetime of navigating volatile political environments.

He understood that public grandstanding could derail delicate negotiations. He valued
incremental progress over dramatic gestures.

Ideologically, Alonto blended:
+ Moro nationalism
+ Islamic ethical framing
«Pragmatic governance

He did not abandon identity-based politics. But he increasingly situated identity within a broader
development and governance agenda.

For him, dignity was inseparable from livelihood.

XII. HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE AND LEGACY

Abul Khayr Dangeal Alonto’s historical significance lies not in a single dramatic moment, but in
the are of his life.

He embodied the transformation of the Moro struggle from armed rebellion to institutional
politics.

He demonstrated that former revolutionaries could become effective administrators.

He showed that loyalty to a cause does not require permanent allegiance to a single tactic.


PAGE 18
His life illustrates a difficult truth:

Liberation movements must eventually learn how to govern—or risk becoming trapped in
endless resistance.

Alonto chose the harder path.

CONCLUSION

Datu Abul Khayr Dangceal Alonto was not a perfect man.
He made controversial choices.

He navigated political compromises.

He shifted alliances.

Yet across five decades of public life, one constant remained: his commitment to the welfare and
dignity of the Bangsamoro people.

From guerrilla training camps to city hall, from autonomy assemblies to diplomatic posts, from
revolutionary meetings to Cabinet deliberations, he carried with him the memory of a wounded
people and the hope that their future could be better.

His story is not only about one man.

It is about a generation that learned—through pain, failure, and perseverance—that building
peace is as demanding as waging war.

And sometimes, even more courageous.

Background and Family
The Alauya family of Bacolod Grande, Lanao del Sur, is one of the most accomplished Bangsamoro families in
modern Philippine public life.
At the center of it all is Justice Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr., a Maranao lawyer and Aleem (Islamic scholar) who served
as Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur in 1989, as Acting Governor from 1992 to 1995, and as Chairman of the Code
Commission on Muslim Laws in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in 1994.
In August 1996, President Fidel V. Ramos appointed him as Jurisconsult in Islamic Law of the Philippines,
making him the first person to hold that office under the Supreme Court of the Philippines.<ref
name="wiki_alauya">Template:Cite web</ref>
The Jurisconsult, created under Presidential Decree 1083 or the Code of Muslim Personal Laws, functions as an
expert advisor to the Supreme Court on matters of Islamic law.<ref name="wiki_alauya" />
He is also a prolific legal author, having written foundational texts on Muslim inheritance law, fundamentals of
Islamic jurisprudence, Islamic penal law, and procedure and evidence under the Muslim Code.<ref
name="wiki_alauya" />
During part of his career, Justice Alauya served as a professor at Umm Al-Qura University in Makkah, Saudi
Arabia, a tenure that would shape the early education and worldview of his youngest daughter.
His children have matched his legacy, each staking out their own "firsts."
Atty. Arifa Alauya-Ala, a Certified Public Accountant and lawyer, is the first Maranao woman to serve as Senior
Assistant Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), the country's central bank.<ref
name="bsp_ala">Template:Cite web</ref>
She is the BSP's lead advocate for Islamic banking and finance, chairing the Inter-Agency Working Group on
Islamic Banking and Finance, and was a key figure in the passage of the Islamic Banking Law (Republic Act No.
11439) in 2019.<ref name="context_ala">Template:Cite web</ref>
In September 2025, she was recognized as a "Woman Influencer in Financial Services Industry" by the World
Financial Innovation Series.<ref name="context_ala" />
Atty. Asma Alauya also serves in the legal services sector of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. [Note: The specific
title of General Legal Counsel attributed to Atty. Asma Alauya could not be independently verified through
available public records at the time of writing. This detail is sourced from family accounts and is subject to
verification.]
Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr., a lawyer and Certified Public Accountant, currently serves as Vice Chancellor for
Administration and Finance of Mindanao State University Main Campus in Marawi City.<ref
name="msu_alauya">Template:Cite web</ref>
Into this family of pioneering lawyers, administrators, and jurists, Dr. Aslama stepped not with a bar examination
but with a stethoscope.

PAGE 3
She became the first doctor in the family and, in doing so, opened an entirely new frontier for the Alauya legacy.
Early Life and Education Abroad
Dr. Aslama spent a significant portion of her early years and formative schooling in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, during
the period when her father was serving as a professor at Umm Al-Qura University.
Growing up between the spiritual heart of the Islamic world and the cultural heartbeat of Marawi City gave her
something few Maranao children of her generation had: a genuinely global perspective, paired with an unshakeable
sense of who she was and where she came from.
From her earliest years in school through college, she was consistently at the top of her class.
She graduated as Valedictorian at every level of her academic journey, from grade school all the way to the College
of Medicine.
Medical Education
Dr. Aslama completed her medical degree at the Mindanao State University College of Medicine, where she made
history as the first Maranao lady Valedictorian of the college.
That achievement alone would have been remarkable, but it was only the opening chapter of a much longer record.
After earning her medical degree from MSU, she pursued residency training at the National Kidney and Transplant
Institute (NKTI) in Metro Manila, then went on to complete fellowship training in pulmonary medicine at the
University of the Philippines.<ref name="hms_feature">Template:Cite web</ref>
She holds the credentials MD, FPCP (Fellow of the Philippine College of Physicians), FPCCP (Fellow of the
Philippine College of Chest Physicians), and FCCP (Fellow of the American College of Chest Physicians).
Medical Career
Clinical Work
Dr. Aslama is a pulmonologist and internal medicine specialist who has built her practice in Iligan City and the
broader Lanao region.
She serves as one of the consultants at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, the only tertiary hospital in Marawi City
serving Lanao del Sur and its neighboring cities and provinces.<ref name="hms_feature" />
She also holds a private pulmonology practice at Mercy Community Hospital and other hospitals in Iligan City.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Aslama worked on the frontlines as a clinician in the respiratory unit of the
internal medicine department at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, treating patients at the height of the health crisis
while simultaneously training resident physicians.
Following her graduation from Harvard Medical School in 2024, she was assigned as medical specialist supervisor
of Station 8 at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, a general medicine ward that routinely handles more patients than its
official capacity, including critical cases when the intensive care unit is full.<ref name="hms_feature" />

PAGE 4
She has been implementing lean management principles in that ward, applying the capstone work she developed at
Harvard to improve patient outcomes and care efficiency at the hospital level.
First Maranao Pulmonologist
Among Dr. Aslama's most significant achievements is a straightforward but historically weighty fact: she is the
first Maranao pulmonologist in the Philippines.
In a region where respiratory diseases, tuberculosis, and pulmonary complications from COVID-19 have placed
enormous pressure on healthcare capacity, having the first Maranao specialist in pulmonary medicine based in the
heart of Lanao is more than a milestone. It's a public health breakthrough.
Leadership in Medicine
Dr. Aslama made history as the first Maranao woman elected President of the Iligan Society of Internists, a
distinction that reflects her standing not just as a clinician but as a recognized leader among her peers in the
medical community.
She currently serves as Vice President of the Philippine College of Chest Physicians, Northern Mindanao Chapter,
continuing to expand Maranao representation in the country's medical leadership landscape.
Harvard Medical School and International Recognition
Between managing her clinical responsibilities and training resident physicians at Amai Pakpak Medical Center,
Dr. Aslama applied to the Harvard Medical School Postgraduate Medical Education's Leadership in Medicine:
Southeast Asia certificate program (now expanded as the Leadership in Medicine: Asia Pacific program).<ref
name="hms_sea">Template:Cite web</ref>
She was accepted.
"I realized that aside from being a clinician, I wanted to learn about leadership, solving problems, and
managing teams." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, as cited by Harvard Medical School, 2024)
The one-year blended certificate program, developed in partnership with Sunway University in Malaysia, combines
in-person workshops (in Bandar Sunway, Selangor and Boston, Massachusetts), pre-recorded lectures, and live
webinars, covering leadership, health care finance, human resource management, quality management, and
organizational change.<ref name="hms_sea" />
In February 2024, Dr. Aslama traveled to Boston for the final in-person workshop and graduation ceremony.
She graduated with distinction.
Harvard Medical School faculty recognized her as one of the top three capstone project proposal authors in her
cohort.
She also received the Excellence Award for her team assignment, an honor recognizing standout performance in
the program's collaborative finance component.<ref name="hms_feature" />

PAGE 5
Her capstone proposal focused on implementing lean management principles to improve cardiopulmonary
resuscitation outcomes in the general medicine ward of Amai Pakpak Medical Center, a practical and immediately
applicable contribution to her home hospital.<ref name="hms_feature" />
"The process of developing this capstone proposal made me realize the many ways in which we can
improve processes in any institution. Starting with a small scope, we can gradually expand until we
cover a larger dimension by integrating all the smaller scopes." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, Harvard
Medical School, 2024)
She is the first Maranao woman to graduate with distinction from a Harvard Medical School postgraduate
certificate program, and the first from her community to earn recognition at that institution's level.
Awards and Distinctions
Dr. Aslama's record of "firsts" spans local, national, and international scales.
Pride of Ranaw Award
The Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur bestows the Pride of Ranaw Award on individuals whose
achievements, integrity, and service bring distinction and honor to the Maranao people.
Dr. Aslama is the first Maranao doctor and pulmonologist to receive this recognition, which she accepted after
completing her Harvard Medical School program.<ref name="hms_feature" />
"I am so happy and grateful for my experience at Harvard Medical School, and my community is so
thankful that I received this training." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, Harvard Medical School, 2024)
Distinguished Public Servant Award (Philippine College of Chest Physicians)
The Philippine College of Chest Physicians (PCCP) confers its Distinguished Public Servant Award on members
who have demonstrated exemplary service, leadership, and significant contributions to the advancement of
pulmonary medicine in the Philippines.
Dr. Aslama is the first Maranao recipient of this award, recognizing her record of clinical service, community
engagement, and healthcare leadership in a medically underserved region.
Valedictorian, MSU College of Medicine
Her distinction as the first Maranao lady Valedictorian of the MSU College of Medicine placed her at the top of
one of Mindanao's most competitive professional schools, a milestone that set the tone for everything that
followed.
Harvard Excellence Award
Her selection as a top-three capstone author and recipient of the Excellence Award for teamwork during the HMS
Leadership in Medicine program marks her as the first Maranao woman honored in that capacity by one of the
world's foremost medical institutions.

PAGE 6
Summary of "Firsts"
The following is a consolidated record of pioneering achievements attributed to Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping:

First Maranao pulmonologist in the Philippines

Government of Lanao del Sur

Medical School
The Alauya Family: A Legacy of Firsts
No article about Dr. Aslama would be complete without acknowledging that her firsts did not happen in a vacuum.
They came from a family that has, across two generations, made a habit of breaking new ground.
Her father, Justice Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr., was the first Jurisconsult in Islamic Law of the Philippines,
appointed by President Fidel V. Ramos in 1996 and serving until 2003. No Maranao lawyer had held that office
before him, and his tenure helped shape the framework of Islamic jurisprudence within the Philippine judiciary.<ref
name="wiki_alauya" />
Her sister, Atty. Arifa Alauya-Ala, is the first Maranao woman to serve as Senior Assistant Governor of the
Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, leading the country's Islamic banking and finance agenda and earning international
recognition as a "Woman Influencer in Financial Services."<ref name="bsp_ala" /><ref name="context_ala" />
Her brother, Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr., serves as Vice Chancellor for Administration and Finance of
Mindanao State University Main Campus, stewarding the finances and administration of one of the largest state
universities in the Philippines.<ref name="msu_alauya" />
Together, the Alauya family represents one of the most decorated Bangsamoro families in the country's institutional
history, with representation across the judiciary, central banking, state university governance, and now medicine.
Dr. Aslama is the youngest, and arguably the one who widened the family's footprint the furthest by entering a field
no Alauya had entered before.
Personal Life
Dr. Aslama is married to Engineer Abdulmojeb Lamping.
They are blessed with twin daughters, Amanah Ayla and Arafah Aneena, whom family accounts describe as
equally talented and intellectually gifted.
She is a proud and self-identified member of the Meranaw tribe, a Muslim Filipino ethnic group native to the
region around Lanao del Sur, known for their rich cultural heritage including the okir art tradition, the malong, and
a deep history of Islamic learning and scholarship.<ref name="hms_feature" />

PAGE 7
Her identity as a Maranao woman, a Muslim, and a daughter of Lanao del Sur runs through her professional
choices, her clinical practice, and her community commitments. She has not left Mindanao behind for a more
prominent career elsewhere. Instead, she has brought Harvard-level training home to the hospitals and patients of
her own people.
Legacy
Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping's career is, at its core, a story about what happens when excellence meets commitment
to community.
She could have taken her credentials, her Harvard certificate, her fellowship training from UP and NKTI, and her
PCCP fellowship, and built a career in Metro Manila or abroad.
She didn't.
She came back to Marawi, to Iligan, to the Lanao region, and she stayed. She treats patients at Amai Pakpak, the
only tertiary hospital serving a city still rebuilding from the 2017 siege. She trains resident physicians. She
manages a private practice. She chairs medical societies. She implements lean healthcare principles in wards that
are perpetually over capacity.
And she does it all as the first Maranao pulmonologist, as the youngest daughter of the country's first Jurisconsult
in Islamic Law, as the sister of the BSP's first Maranao Senior Assistant Governor, as a wife, a mother of twins, and
a Harvard graduate.
"The training that I received in the Leadership in Medicine: Asia Pacific program added valuable
context in my past roles, and it continues to do so in my current position." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-
Lamping, Harvard Medical School, 2024)
That is the measure of her legacy: not just the firsts she collected, but the ones she created space for.

Datumanong A. Sarangani
Datumanong A. Sarangani (September 17, 1946 – 2011) was a
Filipino educator, academic administrator, and scholar from Lanao
del Sur, Philippines. He is best remembered for his forty-five
years of service at Mindanao State University (MSU), where he
served in various capacities — from faculty member, to college
secretary, to dean, to chancellor of two MSU campuses, to
University Secretary, to Secretary to the Board of Regents, and
finally to Executive Vice President (EVP) of the entire MSU
System. He entered MSU in 1962 as one of its first 282 students
and graduated in 1966 as part of its pioneer batch of 63 graduates,
making his personal story almost a mirror image of the
university's own growth.
Within the MSU community, he is widely regarded as the "best
President MSU never had" — a phrase that captures how deeply
he was respected not for the title he held, but for the kind of

Background and Early Life
Datumanong A. Sarangani was born on September 17, 1946, in
Lanao del Sur, a province in what is now the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). He grew
up in a Maranao Muslim community where Islamic tradition and
close-knit clan networks shaped everyday life. Not much has been
formally documented about his parents or siblings, but what is
clear is that he came from a generation of Muslims who had very
limited access to quality higher education in the Philippines.
When Mindanao State University was founded in 1961 through
Republic Act No. 1387, it was created specifically to address that
problem — to bring educational opportunity to Muslim Filipinos
and to test whether Muslim and Christian youth could genuinely
study and live together under one roof. Sarangani walked into that
experiment in June 1962, just a year after MSU opened its doors.
The campus he arrived at was rough by any standard. Electricity
was unreliable. Water supply was inconsistent. Infrastructure was
barely in place. He later described those early years at MSU as a
"no man's land," where students had to tough it out and lean on
each other to get through.<ref name="gcpe">Global Campaign
for Peace Education. (2018, September 5). Teaching peace in the

have become the foundation for one of his most enduring beliefs
about education: that surviving difficulty together builds
something deeper than any classroom lesson alone can offer.
Education
Sarangani earned his undergraduate degree from Mindanao State
University, graduating in April 1966 as part of the institution's
first-ever graduating class of 63 students.<ref
name="msua">Mindanao State University. (n.d.-a). About us:
History of Mindanao State University.
https://www.msumain.edu.ph/about-us/</ref> That milestone was
no small thing — these 63 graduates were proof that MSU's
founding mission was not just a political idea but a reality.
He later pursued advanced studies and earned a Doctor of
Education (Ed.D.), making him one of the early Muslim Filipino
scholars who went through a full academic pipeline — from
pioneer student to doctoral degree holder — at MSU itself. This
put him among the first wave of Muslim Filipino academics
whose credentials were earned entirely within a Philippine state
university context, rather than through foreign scholarships or
metropolitan institutions in Manila.<ref name="msub">Mindanao State University. (n.d.-b). The MSU System
executive vice presidents. https://www.msumain.edu.ph/office-of-the-executive-vice-president/the-msu-system-
executive-vice-presidents/</ref>
Career Overview
Faculty Member and Early Academic Work
After graduation, Sarangani joined the MSU faculty in the College of Social Sciences and Humanities, teaching
sociology and related subjects.<ref name="msua"/> His early teaching years coincided with a turbulent period in
Mindanao — the 1970s and early 1980s saw political upheaval, the declaration of Martial Law, and the rise of the
Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), all of which surrounded MSU even as the university tried to hold on to
its mission of integration.
Throughout this period, he chose to remain with MSU, building his reputation through consistent teaching and
early scholarly work rather than seeking positions elsewhere.
College Secretary and Dean
Before moving into system-wide positions, Sarangani served in middle-level administrative roles as college
secretary and later as dean within MSU.<ref name="msua"/> These roles introduced him to the practical realities
of running an academic unit — faculty evaluation, curriculum oversight, student discipline, and resource

PAGE 4
management. Colleagues noted that even at this stage, he showed a preference for documentation, proper
procedure, and doing things by the book — habits that would define his later career.
Chancellor, MSU–General Santos City (1988)
In 1988, Sarangani was appointed Chancellor of MSU–General Santos City,<ref name="msub"/> one of the
constituent campuses of the growing MSU System. The chancellorship gave him responsibility for campus-level
governance, and he used that platform to emphasize orderly administration, faculty morale, and academic programs
that served the community. His approach to leadership — calm, principled, and transparent — was already visible
at this stage.
Chancellor, MSU–Main Campus, Marawi (1990)
Two years later, in 1990, he moved to the most prominent campus in the system, becoming Chancellor of MSU–
Main Campus in Marawi City.<ref name="msub"/> Marawi was — and still is — the heart of the MSU System
and the symbolic center of Muslim Filipino higher education. As chancellor, he continued to prioritize campus
peace and order, support for social sciences and Islamic studies, and the kind of transparent administrative
processes that reduce room for favoritism or political interference.
University Secretary and Secretary to the Board of Regents (1990)
Also in August 1990, Sarangani took on the dual role of University Secretary and Secretary to the Board of
Regents,<ref name="msub"/> positions that placed him at the center of all official MSU governance. These roles
made him the custodian of MSU's official records, the person who authenticated board resolutions, and the
coordinator of communications across the university's growing number of campuses. In practice, this made him
MSU's institutional memory — the person who knew what had been decided, why, and on what basis.
Executive Vice President, MSU System (1990–2011)
Sarangani served as Executive Vice President of the MSU System from 1990 until his retirement on his sixty-
fifth birthday, September 17, 2011 — a continuous tenure of twenty-one years in the system's top operational role.
<ref name="msub"/> As EVP, he functioned as the chief operating officer of the entire MSU System, assisting the
president in strategic governance and overseeing day-to-day operations across what had grown into an eleven-
campus system — one of the largest state university systems in the Philippines.<ref name="msua"/>
What makes this tenure historically unusual is that he held the EVP position continuously across multiple
presidential administrations, a rare achievement in Philippine public higher education where political transitions
typically bring leadership reshuffles. Each successive MSU president chose to retain him — a reflection of the trust
and credibility he had built across decades.

PAGE 5
Scholarly Work and Intellectual Contributions
Context of Muslim Filipino Scholarship
When Sarangani started writing and doing research, Muslim Filipino scholars were a rare presence in Philippine
academic circles. For a long time, Muslims in Mindanao were more often written about than given the chance to
write for themselves. Sarangani belonged to the generation that began to change that.
His intellectual interests were grounded and practical. Rather than pursuing abstract theoretical work disconnected
from Mindanao's realities, he focused on history and sociology as tools for understanding Muslim communities on
their own terms.
"Islamic Penetration in Mindanao and Sulu" (1974)
His most cited scholarly contribution is the article Islamic Penetration in Mindanao and Sulu, published in 1974
in the Mindanao Journal of the MSU University Research Center.<ref name="sarangani">Sarangani, D. A. (1974).
Islamic penetration in Mindanao and Sulu. Mindanao Journal, 1(1).</ref> The study traces how Islam spread
through the southern Philippines across several centuries through trade, religious missions, and political alliances.
Three things stand out about this work:
1. It pushed back against simplistic histories. The article challenged colonial-era and Eurocentric accounts
that treated Islamic polities in Mindanao and Sulu as peripheral or backward. Instead, it demonstrated that
these societies had sophisticated political and religious institutions long before Spanish colonization arrived.
2. It centered local agency. Rather than portraying Islamization as something done to the people of Mindanao
and Sulu, it showed local rulers and communities actively choosing and shaping how Islam took root in their
societies.
3. It combined history and sociology. While the subject is historical, the article also examined how religious
change intersected with social organization and political authority — an interdisciplinary approach unusual
for its time in this field.<ref name="sarangani"/>
Broader Intellectual Themes
Across his scholarly and professional work, several consistent themes run through Sarangani's thinking:
Islam as a full civilization — He consistently treated Islam not just as a religion of rituals but as a complete
system covering law, governance, ethics, and culture.
Education as the road to dignity — He viewed education as the primary way marginalized communities
could reclaim their voice and place in society.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Integration without forced assimilation — He supported being part of the Philippine nation while insisting
that Muslim Filipino identity had to be respected and preserved, not quietly erased — a balance he saw as
central to MSU's founding purpose.<ref name="msua"/>

PAGE 6
Teaching Philosophy and Mentorship
The Classroom as More Than Instruction
By all accounts from alumni and colleagues, Sarangani was a demanding teacher who also genuinely cared for his
students. He expected intellectual seriousness, but he was also known for being approachable and willing to sit
with a student who needed guidance.<ref name="rnc"/> In his classrooms, sociological theory was tied to the
realities students already knew — clan relations, interfaith tensions, economic hardship, and political exclusion in
Mindanao. The result was that students' own experiences were treated as legitimate subjects of serious inquiry, not
just local color.
The "Survivor" Philosophy
One of his most frequently quoted sayings captures something essential about how he saw education:
"If you survive in MSU, you can survive everywhere."
He wasn't just being dramatic. Early MSU was genuinely difficult — limited electricity, scarce water, sparse
facilities. His point was that the hardships students shared built resilience and taught them how to rely on each
other across religious lines. In his view, the difficulties were not a failure of the institution; they were part of what
made the institution transformative.
Known as "Manong"
Even after becoming one of the most senior officials in the MSU System, Sarangani remained the kind of person
students felt comfortable approaching. Alumni remember visiting his office to talk about graduate school plans and
career paths.<ref name="rnc"/> He was widely known as Manong — a Filipino term of respect that roughly
translates as "respected elder brother" — a form of address that reflects the relational, not just formal, authority he
held.
Mentorship That Outlasted His Time at MSU
Graduates mentored by Sarangani went on to careers in academia, government, and civil society. During his
retirement tribute, many of them showed up to say so publicly.<ref name="rnc"/> That kind of showing-up is its
own kind of measurement — a sign that what he gave them went beyond what could be graded.
MSU and the Peace Education Mandate
MSU as a "Social Laboratory"
Sarangani consistently described MSU as a "social laboratory" — a place where peaceful coexistence between
Muslims and Christians wasn't just talked about but actually lived out in dormitories, classrooms, and campus life.
<ref name="gcpe"/> He was an ardent defender of MSU's practice of assigning Muslim and Christian students as
roommates, viewing daily interaction as one of the most powerful tools available for reducing prejudice and
building genuine understanding.<ref name="gcpe"/>

PAGE 7
From a sociological standpoint, this practice aligns closely with intergroup contact theory, which holds that
sustained, equal-status contact between groups reduces prejudice over time. Sarangani understood this intuitively
from his own student experience, even if he articulated it through the lens of lived experience rather than academic
theory.
Keeping Peace During Instability
His career unfolded against a backdrop of chronic conflict in Mindanao — the Moro insurgency, martial law, cycles
of peace talks and renewed hostilities, and eventually the Marawi Siege in the year following his death. Through it
all, he consistently worked to keep MSU's campus from becoming an extension of the conflict outside its gates.
As chancellor and later as EVP, he prioritized student safety, institutional neutrality, and procedural fairness during
periods of tension.<ref name="rnc"/> Colleagues described him as measured and calm in deliberations — a quality
that mattered enormously in environments where a poorly handled campus incident could have serious
consequences.
Peace Education in the Curriculum
During his EVP tenure, MSU strengthened its programs in peace and development studies and Islamic education.
<ref name="msua"/> Sarangani supported these not as peripheral additions but as expressions of MSU's core
purpose. He saw peace education not as a specialty for specialists but as something woven into the university's
entire reason for existing.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Institutional Growth Under His Watch
During Sarangani's two decades as EVP, the MSU System grew from a smaller network of campuses into a full
eleven-campus system — one of the largest in the country.<ref name="msua"/> From its first graduating class of
63 students in 1966, MSU had produced approximately 150,000 graduates by 2018, a substantial portion of whom
passed through the system during his watch.<ref name="gcpe"/>
The EVP's office under his leadership played a central role in harmonizing academic calendars and policies across
those campuses, ensuring that growth did not come at the cost of coherence or quality. Programs were expanded to
include medicine, law, education, engineering, and information technology, all while maintaining compliance with
national accreditation standards.<ref name="msua"/>
By the early 2000s, MSU was nationally recognized as:
A major producer of Muslim Filipino professionals across a wide range of fields
A regional research institution with its own scholarly tradition
A working model of peace-oriented higher education in a conflict-affected area<ref name="gcpe"/>
Governance Philosophy
Sarangani's approach to running things was built around a few consistent principles:
Rules over personalities. He believed that institutions survive when decisions are grounded in documented
policies rather than whoever happens to be in charge at the moment.
Quiet influence. He exercised authority through persuasion, documentation, and institutional consistency
rather than through spectacle or politics.<ref name="rnc"/>

PAGE 8
Mission first. He consistently framed MSU's purpose as service to marginalized communities — especially
Muslim Filipinos — and held that standard up as the measure against which any institutional decision should
be judged.<ref name="msua"/>
His governance style explains why multiple MSU presidents, across different administrations and different political
climates, chose to keep him in place. He was, in a very practical sense, the person who made continuity possible.
Honors and Recognition
MSU Rawaten (Model) Outstanding Alumnus Award (2011)
In 2011, the year of his retirement, Sarangani received the MSU Rawaten Outstanding Alumnus Award, which
recognizes graduates whose lives embody MSU's ideals of service, excellence, and integration.<ref name="rnc"/>
That a pioneer student and pioneer graduate of MSU received this recognition from the same institution was fitting
in a way that is hard to manufacture — it was genuinely circular, in the best sense of the word.
Board of Regents Retirement Tribute (September 17, 2011)
Upon his retirement on his sixty-fifth birthday, the MSU Board of Regents formally honored him for his forty-
five years of service.<ref name="rnc"/> During the tribute, he was publicly acknowledged for having served as
Chancellor of MSU–General Santos City, Chancellor of MSU–Main Campus, University Secretary, Secretary to
the Board of Regents, and Executive Vice President of the MSU System. He was described in official tributes as
"almost synonymous with Mindanao State University."<ref name="rnc"/>
The "Best President MSU Never Had"
Perhaps the most revealing recognition Sarangani received was informal and unplanned: peers and alumni across
generations consistently called him the "best President MSU never had".<ref name="rnc"/> The phrase is not a
complaint about an opportunity denied. It is a recognition that his influence, competence, and moral authority were
of presidential caliber — and that his choice to lead quietly from within was itself a form of leadership the
institution needed more than a title.
Challenges and Constraints
Structural Challenges
Sarangani built his career at an institution perpetually working under difficult conditions — chronic budget
limitations, infrastructure deficiencies, and security risks tied to regional conflict that never fully went away.<ref
name="gcpe"/> None of these were problems he created, and none of them derailed him. His response was to favor
steady, incremental improvement over risky expansionism, and to prioritize institutional stability as an end in itself,
not just as a means to something flashier.

PAGE 9
A Career Free of Public Controversy
A review of available institutional records and media accounts reveals no documented allegations of misconduct,
corruption, or abuse of authority throughout his forty-five years of service.<ref name="rnc"/><ref name="msub"/>
In Philippine public higher education, where administrative scandals are not uncommon, this record is itself a form
of distinction — a sign of consistent procedural integrity and ethical self-discipline.
The Trade-Off Between Administration and Research
One area where Sarangani's career reflects a common tension in higher education leadership is scholarly output.
The record of his publications is modest in volume. This is not unusual for someone who carried the kind of
administrative load he did for as long as he did — the work of institution-building tends to crowd out the time
needed for sustained research.<ref name="msub"/> What he gave to scholarship, he gave earlier; the second half of
his career, he gave to governance.
Legacy
An Institutional Type: The Steward
Within Philippine higher education history, Sarangani represents what might be called the institutional steward —
a kind of leader who is not always the one at the front of the room but without whom institutions do not hold
together across generations.<ref name="msub"/> These figures are often underrepresented in official histories,
because they rarely produce the dramatic moments that make for easy narrative. What they produce instead is
durability — the kind of thing you only fully appreciate when it is gone.
Contribution to Muslim Filipino Professional Class
MSU has been one of the main pipelines through which Muslim Filipinos entered the professional world in the
Philippines — as teachers, engineers, doctors, lawyers, administrators, and scholars.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Sarangani's life is a symbol of that transformation. He was not born into a world where that path was obvious or
easy, and he walked it anyway, and then spent the rest of his life holding the door open for others.
Memory as Institutional Standard
The persistence of tributes to him — phrases like "almost synonymous with MSU" and "best President MSU never
had" — are not just nostalgic remembrances.<ref name="rnc"/> They are ongoing statements about what MSU
values in its leaders. To remember him in this way is to say: this is the kind of person this institution should aspire
to produce and attract.
That is perhaps his most durable contribution — not any single policy or decision, but the standard his life sets for
those who come after.

PAGE 10
Death
Dr. Datumanong A. Sarangani retired on September 17, 2011, his sixty-fifth birthday, after forty-five years of
uninterrupted service to Mindanao State University. He passed away in 2011. The circumstances of his passing are
not detailed in available institutional records, but his retirement tribute — attended by colleagues, alumni, and
university officials — was itself a form of farewell that few people in any institution ever receive.

Salipada Saud Tamano
Salipada Saud Tamano (also known by the honorific Kaka
Ipad) was a Maranao educator, policy thinker, and institution-
builder from Tugaya, Lanao del Sur, in the southern Philippines.
He is recognized as one of the most consequential figures in the
history of Islamic higher education in the Philippines, serving as
both Dean and Chancellor of the King Faisal Center for Islamic,
Arabic and Asian Studies at Mindanao State University (MSU),
and later as Regional Secretary of the Department of
Education, Culture and Sports of the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (ARMM). His intellectual and administrative
career spanned the principal institutional arenas of Muslim
Filipino public life: the university, the regional bureaucracy, and
national policy discourse on Muslim Mindanao education
reform.
Tamano's significance in Muslim Filipino history rests less on a
single dramatic act than on the cumulative reshaping of
institutions — so that Muslim Filipino students, teachers, and
scholars could move through them with dignity and on terms
consistent with their own cultural identity. He pursued what
scholars of Muslim Mindanao governance have described as
institutional reformism: the transformation of existing state and
academic structures to accommodate Muslim history, culture,
and aspirations, rather than a wholesale rejection of those
structures.<ref>Macapado A. Muslim, The Moro Armed Struggle
in the Philippines: The Nonviolent Autonomy Alternative
(Marawi City: Office of the President, Mindanao State
University, 1994).</ref>
His published book, Educational Visions for Muslim Mindanao,
issued under the ARMM Regional Department of Education,
Culture and Sports, remains one of the few policy-oriented
works by a Muslim Filipino educator to address systematically

Early life and background
Tugaya and Maranao intellectual culture
Salipada S. Tamano was born and raised in Tugaya, a municipality situated on the western shore of Lake Lanao in
Lanao del Sur. Tugaya occupies a distinctive position in Maranao collective memory as one of the oldest centers of
Maranao craftsmanship and Islamic culture. The town is most widely known for its centuries-old tradition of okir
— the intricate geometric and arabesque wood-and-metal carving that distinguishes Maranao architecture, dress,
and ceremonial objects — but it was equally a community in which Islamic learning and religious authority carried
deep social weight.<ref>Nagasura T. Madale, The Maranao (Manila: Solidaridad Publishing House, 1997), pp. 12–
34.</ref>
In Maranao society, as in Islamic societies more broadly, the scholar-leader — a figure combining religious
learning with social standing — occupied a central role. Mosque-based Qur'anic instruction, oral transmission of
genealogical and legal tradition, and a social ethic that valued religious knowledge shaped the character of Tugaya's
communities long before any modern school was established there. This environment supplied the moral
foundation for Tamano's later reform work: the conviction that to improve a people's schools is to honor their
deepest values, not to displace them.
