By the middle decades of the twentieth century, Maranao families of means had begun directing their most capable
sons toward overseas higher education. Egypt, and Cairo in particular, had become the preferred destination, owing
to the presence of Al-Azhar University — the oldest institution of higher Islamic learning in the world — and the
newer state universities that combined Islamic formation with modern academic disciplines.<ref>Samuel K. Tan,
Internationalization of the Bangsamoro Struggle (Quezon City: University of the Philippines Press, 1993), pp. 55–
72.</ref>
Education and transnational formation
Ain Shams University, Cairo
Tamano enrolled at Ain Shams University — one of Egypt's major research universities, distinct from Al-Azhar —
where he pursued a Master of Education.<ref>Ashary S. Tamano, Salipada S. Tamano: Life, Work, and Historical
Significance, unpublished research manuscript (2024).</ref> His thesis examined the educational problems of
Muslim Filipinos in the Philippines. Even at this early stage of his career, Muslim Filipino marginalization — its
structural roots and potential remedies — was the organizing problem of his intellectual life.
Cairo in the 1960s and early 1970s was an unusually generative environment for a student interested in the
relationship between Islamic education and modern statecraft. Egypt then served as a crossroads for debates
reverberating across the Muslim world: about the proper relationship of religion and governance, about the
compatibility of Islamic education with scientific training, and about what postcolonial nations owed their
minorities and indigenous cultural institutions. Students from Southeast Asia, West Africa, and the Middle East
exchanged experiences of colonization, mission education, and the struggle to recover cultural self-determination
through schooling.<ref>Anthony Bubalo and Greg Fealy, Joining the Caravan? The Middle East, Islamism and
Indonesia (Sydney: Lowy Institute for International Policy, 2005), pp. 1–30.</ref>
Comparative influences
Among Tamano's fellow Southeast Asian students were Malaysians and Indonesians whose countries were already
experimenting with models for integrating Islamic schools into national education systems. Malaysia's expanding
network of state-funded religious schools and Indonesia's pesantren tradition — boarding schools offering classical
Islamic instruction alongside public school curricula — offered working examples that Islamic education and
modern bureaucracy need not be treated as irreconcilable. These comparative observations would surface decades
later in Tamano's arguments for a systematic, state-supported approach to madrasah integration in the Philippines.
Marriage in Cairo
In Cairo, Tamano met and married Marlene Hofer Tamano, a graduate student who later earned her own master's
degree in management at Cairo University.<ref>Ashary S. Tamano, unpublished research manuscript (2024).</ref>
Marlene Hofer Tamano later became a dean and faculty member at MSU and was recognized with a TOWNS
Award (Ten Outstanding Women in the Nation's Service), one of the Philippines' most distinguished civic honors
for professional women.

Career at Mindanao State University
Return to Mindanao
When Tamano returned to the Philippines in the early 1970s, Mindanao was entering one of the most violent and
politically consequential periods of its modern history. Armed conflict between Moro secessionist movements and
the Marcos government had turned vast stretches of Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao, and Cotabato into contested
territory. Whole communities were displaced; schools were shuttered; the social fabric of Muslim Mindanao was
under severe strain.<ref>Eliseo R. Mercado, "Culture, Economics and Revolt in Mindanao: The Origins of the
MNLF and the Politics of Moro Separatism," in Armed Separatism in Southeast Asia, ed. Lim Joo-Jock and Vani S.
(Singapore: Institute of Southeast Asian Studies, 1984), pp. 150–181.</ref>
Into this environment, Mindanao State University occupied a peculiar but critical position. Established on
September 1, 1961, through Republic Act No. 1387, MSU had been conceived by the national government as a
social laboratory for integration — a place where Filipino Muslims, Christians, and indigenous peoples could
receive quality higher education and develop the mutual understanding the state hoped would contain ethnic and
religious tensions in the south.<ref>Mindanao State University, Wikipedia,
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao_State_University (accessed March 2026).</ref> Tamano joined MSU's
academic community and rose progressively through its ranks, his Cairo credentials positioning him as precisely
the kind of faculty the university needed as it sought to deepen its engagement with Islamic academic traditions.
King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and Asian Studies
The centerpiece of Tamano's career at MSU was his leadership of the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and
Asian Studies — an academic unit established through Saudi Arabian support and recognized as the first
government institution in the Philippines to offer formal programs in Islamic and Arabic studies at the university
level.<ref>Mindanao State University, Graduate Program Department – King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and
Asian Studies, https://www.msumain.edu.ph/graduate-program-department-kfciaas/ (accessed March 2026).</ref>
He served the Center successively as Dean and Chancellor.
Tamano's leadership philosophy rejected two equally inadequate approaches: the purely devotional model, in which
Islamic studies functioned as congregational religious instruction disconnected from critical inquiry; and the
ornamental model, in which Arabic and Islamic programs were offered as tokens of cultural sensitivity without the
faculty development, research culture, and institutional resources to render them genuinely competitive. Under his
direction, the Center positioned Islamic and Arabic studies as fully academic disciplines held to the same standards
of rigor as any other university subject, while remaining grounded in the classical intellectual heritage of the
Islamic tradition. Faculty were encouraged to pursue advanced degrees — many of them abroad — and the Center
cultivated working relationships with Middle Eastern universities providing both visiting scholar arrangements and
graduate training opportunities.
The King Faisal Mosque as civic space
The King Faisal Mosque within MSU, which came under the Center's broader stewardship, served a function
extending well beyond its strictly religious purpose. Under Tamano's tenure it functioned as a venue for public
lectures, a meeting ground for Muslim and non-Muslim leaders, and a visible assertion that Islam had a permanent
and legitimate place within Philippine public institutions.<ref>Thomas M. McKenna, Muslim Rulers and Rebels:
Everyday Politics and Armed Separatism in the Southern Philippines (Berkeley: University of California Press,

Published work and policy framework
Educational Visions for Muslim Mindanao
Tamano's most systematic intellectual contribution was committed to writing in Educational Visions for Muslim
Mindanao, published under the ARMM Regional Department of Education, Culture and Sports.<ref>Salipada S.
Tamano, Educational Visions for Muslim Mindanao (Cotabato City: ARMM Regional Department of Education,
Culture and Sports, n.d.).</ref> The work addressed the central structural problem in Muslim Filipino education:
the coexistence of two separate, largely unconnected systems — the national public school network and the
network of madrasah (Islamic schools) — whose graduates could rarely move between them.
Madrasah integration without assimilation
At the heart of Tamano's argument was the position that madrasah should be integrated into the national education
system without losing the religious and cultural character that gave them their purpose and community support. He
rejected outright absorption — the replacement of Islamic curricula with secular ones — as a form of cultural
erasure that would produce neither better education nor social peace. He was equally critical of the status quo, in
which madrasah graduates found themselves unable to access higher education or stable employment because their
credentials went unrecognized.<ref>Urangutan P. Pangcoga, "Islamic Education in the Philippines: Problems and
Prospects," Philippine Social Sciences and Humanities Review 58, no. 1–4 (1994): 1–25.</ref>
His proposed framework had three layers:
1. Formal recognition — madrasah credentials had to be acknowledged by the state as legitimate educational
qualifications.
2. Regulated standards — not to undermine madrasah autonomy, but to ensure graduates met the academic
benchmarks required for educational mobility.
3. Resourcing — any integration program lacking dedicated budget lines, trained teachers, and appropriate
instructional materials was doomed to remain policy on paper rather than reality in classrooms.
Teacher formation and professional certification
Tamano gave sustained attention to the preparation of teachers, arguing that no curriculum reform — however well
designed — could take root without a cadre of educators trained in both Islamic content and modern pedagogical
methods. His proposals included dedicated teacher-training institutes, formal certification systems for Arabic and
Islamic studies teachers, and career pathways placing these educators on equivalent footing with counterparts in
other subjects.
Access to higher education
The third dimension of Tamano's vision concerned pathways into university. He argued that madrasah graduates of
demonstrated academic ability should be able to enter MSU and other universities' Islamic and Arabic programs
directly, supported by scholarships and supplementary programs in science and mathematics where needed. This
position rested on a conviction that the purpose of education — including Islamic education — was to cultivate

Curriculum as political terrain
One of Tamano's most consequential and enduring arguments concerned the political character of school curricula.
He held that curricula are never neutral — that they transmit historical memory, shape moral frameworks, and
communicate to children which communities and which ways of life are worthy of dignity. Philippine national
curricula, designed in Manila for a predominantly Christian population, had historically transmitted a version of
national history in which Muslim Filipinos appeared — when they appeared at all — as a problem to be managed
rather than a community with its own centuries-long record of political organization, trade, scholarship, and
governance.<ref>Cesar Adib Majul, Muslims in the Philippines (Quezon City: University of the Philippines Press,
1973), pp. 1–15.</ref>
Tamano pushed, within both MSU and the ARMM-DECS, for the substantive inclusion of Islamic Mindanao's
history in regional curricula: the pre-colonial sultanates, Maranao and Maguindanao contributions to Philippine
governance and literature, and the Arabic language as a living heritage language rather than a religious curiosity.
He framed this not as a sectarian demand but as a prerequisite for the genuine national integration that the
Philippine state claimed to want. Later national policies — particularly the Arabic Language and Islamic Values
Education (ALIVE) program and the eventual formal recognition and standardization of madrasah education under
the Department of Education — moved in directions consistent with Tamano's earlier advocacy.
Service in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
Establishment of the ARMM
The Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was created through Republic Act No. 6734, signed by President
Corazon Aquino on August 1, 1989, and ratified through a plebiscite on November 17, 1989, in which four
provinces voted in favor: Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao, Sulu, and Tawi-Tawi.<ref>Republic Act No. 6734, "An Act
Providing for an Organic Act for the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao," Official Gazette of the Republic
of the Philippines, https://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/1989/08/01/republic-act-no-6734/ (accessed March 2026).
</ref>
Regional Secretary, DECS-ARMM
Tamano accepted the position of Regional Secretary of the Department of Education, Culture and Sports
(DECS-ARMM), moving from the relative shelter of university administration into the harder terrain of regional
governance.<ref>Marly Hofer-Hasim, Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marly_Hofer%E2%80%93Hasim
(accessed March 2026).</ref>
What he found was a system operating under severe constraint: schools damaged or destroyed during years of
conflict; acute teacher shortages across the region; fiscal transfers from the national government that were neither
predictable nor adequate; a bureaucratic culture poorly prepared for the planning and evaluation functions that
genuine autonomy demanded; and patronage networks that complicated any attempt to make personnel and
program decisions on strictly professional grounds.

Administrative philosophy
Tamano's response was what the institutional record reflects as incremental institutional consolidation — a
deliberate choice to build internal capacity rather than pursue sweeping reforms that the fragile system could not
sustain. He worked to clarify regional authority over curriculum, establish functioning planning and monitoring
units within the DECS-ARMM, and strengthen the relationship between the regional education office and MSU,
which he regarded as an indispensable technical resource for a region that lacked many of its own research and
training capacities.
His handling of the madrasah question at the regional level reflected the same pragmatic gradualism. He insisted
that recognition, without accompanying regulation and resourcing, was meaningless — a point he pressed
repeatedly against those who regarded formal acknowledgment of madrasah credentials as an end in itself rather
than a first step in a longer process. He called this inadequate alternative symbolic integration: policies that
recognized institutions on paper while leaving them unfunded in practice.
Stance on armed conflict
Tamano's career unfolded during the height of Moro armed resistance against the Philippine state. He did not join
armed resistance movements.<ref>W.K. Che Man, Muslim Separatism: The Moros of Southern Philippines and the
Malays of Southern Thailand (Singapore: Oxford University Press, 1990).</ref>
This choice should not be read as political indifference or accommodation to state power. Tamano acknowledged,
in his academic work and public addresses, that colonial governance — both Spanish and American — had
systematically disrupted indigenous Muslim institutions, and that postcolonial development policy had reproduced
many colonial assumptions about Muslim communities. His critique of structural exclusion was neither mild nor
evasive.
His divergence from the armed movements was a difference of method, not of diagnosis. He held that the most
durable form of self-determination was the one built into everyday institutions: into who teaches the children, what
they are taught, which languages they learn in, and which histories they are shown. No political settlement,
however favorable its terms, would produce genuine Muslim Filipino empowerment if the schools, universities,
and teacher-training programs remained incapable of sustaining a Muslim Filipino scholarly and professional class.
In this way, Tamano represents a non-combatant tradition of Moro resistance — struggle pursued through
institutional transformation rather than armed confrontation.
Historical significance
Position in Muslim Filipino intellectual history
Salipada S. Tamano belongs to a tradition of Muslim Filipino thinkers — less visible in popular historical memory
than warriors and politicians — who pursued self-determination through institutional transformation. This tradition
runs from the pre-colonial ulama who built the sultanates' legal and administrative cultures through the colonial-era
reformers who argued for Muslim participation in Philippine public life, to the post-war generation of educators
and professionals who moved into MSU, the civil service, and eventually the autonomous regional government.
Within that lineage, Tamano occupies a specific niche: the scholar-bureaucrat who could move with equal fluency
between the world of Islamic academic tradition and the world of modern educational administration. This dual
competence allowed him to translate an Islamic educational vision into the language of curricular standards, budget
lines, and institutional policy — something neither pure administrators nor pure religious scholars could do alone.

By framing Muslim Filipino marginalization as a structural and policy problem amenable to structural and policy
solutions — rather than as an inevitable consequence of cultural difference — Tamano contributed to a gradual
repositioning of Muslim Filipinos in national discourse: less as a problem to be managed, more as partners whose
educational development was a national responsibility and a national interest.<ref>Patricio N. Abinales, Making
Mindanao: Cotabato and Davao in the Formation of the Philippine Nation-State (Manila: Ateneo de Manila
University Press, 2000), pp. 185–222.</ref>
Influence on national policy
Later national education policies — the ALIVE program, the formal recognition and standardization of madrasah
education under the Department of Education, and the curriculum localization frameworks adopted in the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) — moved in directions that Tamano had been
advocating for decades. He belongs to the category of foundational thinkers whose influence enters policy through
slow intellectual pressure rather than direct attribution.
Acknowledged constraints
A balanced assessment of Tamano's career must acknowledge what his reform work did not fully achieve.
Madrasah mainstreaming in the Philippines remains incomplete. Madrasah quality across BARMM varies
considerably. Teacher shortages persist. The certification and professional development pipeline he envisioned has
been constructed only partially and unevenly. Budget allocations for Islamic and Arabic education remain subject
to annual political negotiation rather than structural guarantee.
These gaps reflect the structural difficulties of changing institutions shaped by decades of underfunding, political
patronage, and the ongoing effects of armed conflict — not the inadequacy of Tamano's intellectual framework.
Family
Marlene Hofer Tamano
Tamano's wife, Marlene Hofer Tamano, built her own distinguished career at MSU, serving as a dean and
receiving the TOWNS Award (Ten Outstanding Women in the Nation's Service) — a recognition reserved for
Filipino women who have made exceptional contributions to their professions and communities. She earned her
master's degree in management at Cairo University.
